extracted.intended_audience: Coast Guard managers, contracting officers, procurement officials, and researchers studying OMB A-76 contracting and cost performance
extracted.subtask_short: A-76 contracting evaluation for Coast Guard
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and analytic criteria for evaluating Coast Guard commercial activities contracted out under OMB Circular A-76, including how to prepare Performance Work Statements, develop a Most Efficient Organization (MEO), compare contractor costs to in‑house costs, and identify causes of contractor cost increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals of OMB Circular A-76
rubrics_metrics.description: The goals of A-76 were to: - Achieve economy and enhance productivity. - Retain Government functions (as defined in A-76) in house. - Rely on the commercial sector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These goals frame decisions about whether to retain functions in-house or contract them out; they are the policy objectives against which savings and program effects are measured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developing an accurate and comprehensive Performance Work Statement (PWS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the Performance Work Statement (PWS) specifies exactly what is required under the contract, it must be accurate and comprehensively describe all the work which the function performs. To be effective, the PWS would also need to be written clearly and concisely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because both the MEO and contractors base bids on the PWS, errors or omissions can lead to cost growth after award. PWS development requires careful study of tasks, frequencies, and historical workload; rushed or poorly trained authors increase risk of later cost changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: PWS must provide accurate historical data
rubrics_metrics.description: Finally, the PWS must provide accurate historical data. This affords potential bidders some idea of the nature and frequency of Level II and Level III Work to be expected, and gives them the basis for developing their price proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical data are used by bidders to price unplanned (Level II/III) work; absent/poor data cause underpricing and later contract modifications or cost growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorize work: Standing (Scheduled) vs Unscheduled
rubrics_metrics.description: In developing the PWS, work was broken down into two broad categories — Standing, or Scheduled Work, and Unscheduled Work. Standing or Scheduled Work is of a recurrent nature, and can be planned for in advance. Unscheduled Work is that type of work which cannot be accurately planned for, but can be expected to occur over time (repairs, installations, modifications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct categorization enables appropriate pricing mechanisms (e.g., fixed-price inclusion for scheduled work) and helps define expected contractor responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work level definitions (Level I, II, III) and pricing approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Work is also broken into three work levels. All Standing Work is Level I Work, which is quantified at a fixed price. Level II Work includes all repairs up to $25,000; this is also quantified at a fixed price. All other Unscheduled Work is Level III Work, which is negotiated as performance dictates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifying levels and thresholds in the PWS clarifies which tasks are included at contract price vs handled via negotiated modifications or delivery orders, reducing ambiguity that can lead to cost growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Most Efficient Organization (MEO) development and costing
rubrics_metrics.description: From the PWS, the Government then determined the best organizational structure, staffing, and operating procedures for what was defined as the Most Efficient Organization (MEO). Following this, the costs of operating the function under the MEO were developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MEO is the Government's in‑house baseline and forms the government's offer in a competition. Accurate staffing, job classification, and cost estimation for the MEO are critical for a valid contractor-vs-government cost comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare contractor offer cost to MEO cost
rubrics_metrics.description: The PWS was then used in a competition with private industry, comparing an offeror’s cost to perform the activity with the MEO's costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The central evaluation metric for award and later cost-effectiveness assessments is whether contractor performance costs less than an adjusted Government MEO; this comparison must account for changes over time to determine continued cost-effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management Study requirements and skilled staffing
rubrics_metrics.description: Units were assigned deadlines for completing a Management Study, which required an in-depth analysis of the function. Ideally, personnel thoroughly familiar with A-76 should have been assigned to each unit for the express purpose of conducting the Management Study and developing the PWS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inadequately trained or unfamiliar personnel often resulted in late or poor PWS development, delayed decisions, and errors that can cause cost increases. Proper training and dedicated staff are evaluation criteria for study quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection/exemption criteria for functions to include in CA inventory
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational units such as Coast Guard cutters capable of towing disabled vessels were exempted from consideration, since they also perform many Government functions such as Law Enforcement and Military Readiness. Remaining functions were listed in the inventory and forwarded for departmental/OMB review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear rules for exemptions ensure only truly commercial activities are competed; improper inclusion of mixed or inherently governmental functions can lead to inappropriate contracts and later cost or performance problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicitation approach: competitive vs set-aside
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the functions contracted out, 16 were conducted on a competitive basis, while 25 were reserved for small, disadvantaged businesses under the SBA 8(a) set-aside program. All contracts awarded competitively were solicited as invitations for bid (IFB) with the Government also a bidder based on the MEO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of solicitation type (competitive IFB, negotiated, small business set-aside) affects contractor pool, pricing, and potential for protests or performance issues; selection of solicitation approach is therefore a criterion in the contracting process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract drafting: include performance incentives and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: As the contract is written, there is no method to take deductions for sub-standard performance. If the contractor does not perform to the level specified in the contract, the Contracting Officer does not have many alternatives to provide an incentive to improve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including incentives, liquidated damages, or other remedies in the contract provides mechanisms to enforce performance and discourage cost/quality degradation; absence of such clauses is a design flaw likely to increase costs or reduce quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control and accountability of Government Furnished Equipment (GFE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Control over Government Furnished Equipment was lacking. Tools used by the former Government organization were made available to the contractor. However, there was no corresponding system to maintain accountability of these items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A formal inventory/ accountability system for GFE/GFM should be specified in the PWS/contract to avoid misappropriation, schedule slippages due to delayed GFE delivery, and unanticipated replacement costs for missing items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract administration support: active ACO/COTR engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Contracting Officer Technical Representative (COTR) and Housing Officer identified a lack of administrative contract support from the Administrative Contracting Officer (ACO). The local ACO previously visited the project often; the current ACO had never visited the site. Contract interpretations are subject to inordinate delays or are never received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely, local contract administration, site visits, and rapid contract interpretation are criteria for effective post-award administration; absence contributes to disputes, delays, and cost growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for logistical factors (distance, delivery time) affecting performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Delivery of GFE and Government Furnished Material is difficult to plan for. Perhaps because of the distance and the routing that GFE/GFM must travel to get to Hawaii, it takes a long time for these items to arrive from the date of order. Of course, late arrival causes schedule slippages, which can result in cost increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or drafting contracts, account for supply-chain/delivery lead times and geographic logistics as explicit risk factors and include mitigation (spare stocks, scheduling allowances, contingency funds) to reduce later cost growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define roles, authorities, and responsibilities clearly for contract stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: The responsibilities of the Housing Officer, the assistant Housing Officer, and the COTR have not been clearly defined to the contractor. They have been tasked by various members of the Housing Office, but are not sure if that person actually had the authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PWS and contract documents should specify individual responsibilities and authorities to reduce miscommunication, unauthorized directions, and disputes that can lead to rework and cost increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of contract modifications and tracking extra work
rubrics_metrics.description: Since contract performance began, twelve contract modifications have been issued (examples: change orders for additional work, wage determination changes, one-year extensions, incorporation of contractor proposals for replacements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track and limit use of post-award modifications by ensuring PWS completeness and using appropriate contract types; excessive modifications indicate initial scope/pricing problems and are predictors of cost growth.
